<snippet id="36414908">Title: Comparative Effectiveness of Device-Aided Therapies on Quality of Life and Off-Time in Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis.
Authors: Antonini, Angelo, Pahwa, Rajesh, Odin, Per et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: CNS drugs
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
Research comparing levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI) for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) is lacking. This network meta-analysis (NMA) assessed the comparative effectiveness of LCIG, DBS, CSAI and best medical therapy (BMT) in reducing off-time and improving quality of life (QoL) in patients with advanced PD.
METHODS
A systematic literature review was conducted for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational and interventional studies from January 2003 to September 2019. Data extracted at baseline and 6 months were off-time, as reported by diary or Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part IV item 39, and QoL, as reported by Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39/PDQ-8). Bayesian NMA was performed to estimate pooled treatment effect sizes and to rank treatments in order of effectiveness.
RESULTS
A total of 22 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria (n = 2063 patients): four RCTs, and 16 single-armed, one 2-armed and one 3-armed prospective studies. Baseline mean age was between 55.5-70.9 years, duration of PD was 9.1-15.3 years, off-time ranged from 5.4 to 8.7 h/day in 9 studies, and PDQ scores ranged from 28.8 to 67.0 in 19 studies. <snippet id="21351823">Title: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel for treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
Authors: Fernandez, H H, Odin, P | Year: 2011 | Journal: Current medical research and opinion
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Levodopa is the mainstay of Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment, but is often eventually associated with disabling motor complications in patients with advanced PD. The inability of perorally administered levodopa to provide more physiologic continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) is a leading hypothesis to explain these complications.
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the cumulative efficacy and safety, and re-evaluate the role, of levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion in treatment of advanced PD patients experiencing levodopa-associated motor complications, through its purported mechanism for providing CDS.
METHODS
Literature searches in the MEDLINE/PubMed database were used to identify peer-reviewed publications examining the role of CDS in levodopa-associated motor complications and pharmacologic strategies for CDS, focusing on LCIG infusion for advanced PD patients.

LCIG, an aqueous gel, is continuously infused (daytime only or 24 h) via a portable pump and tube permanently inserted into the duodenum through percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). LCIG infusion provides stable levodopa plasma levels, which are significantly less variable than those with oral levodopa. Clinical trials indicate LCIG may significantly improve motor complications (reduction of time in 'off' and time in 'on with dyskinesias'), motor scores using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), non-motor symptomatology (Non-motor Symptom Scale) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in advanced PD patients. <snippet id="27138916">Title: Levodopa-Carbidopa Intestinal Gel in Patients with Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review.
Authors: Wirdefeldt, Karin, Odin, Per, Nyholm, Dag | Year: 2016 | Journal: CNS drugs
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is available in several countries for the treatment of advanced levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease (PD) with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesia when other treatments have not given satisfactory results.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to summarize the present evidence base for LCIG therapy through a systematic review of the literature.
METHODS
Studies were identified from the PubMed and EMBASE databases up to 12 March 2016 using the following search terms: Parkinson disease, duodopa, levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, LCIG, l-dopa infusion, levodopa infusion, duodenal l-dopa infusion, and duodenal levodopa infusion. Data extraction focused on whether LCIG therapy improves motor and non-motor outcomes as well as quality of life in PD patients compared with conventional therapy, apomorphine infusion, or deep brain stimulation. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies, with or without a control group, that included more than ten patients were included. The search was limited to peer-reviewed articles published in full in the English language and involving humans.
RESULTS
Infusion of LCIG reduced "off" time, increased "on" time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improved quality of life in three RCTs (one double-blind). Open-label follow-ups confirm these findings. The data evaluating long-term efficacy and safety are still limited.
CONCLUSIONS
The quality of evidence that LCIG is effective in reducing fluctuating motor symptoms and improving quality of life is moderate. Quality of evidence for reduction of non-motor symptoms is very low. Safety issues mainly relate to the intestinal infusion system. LCIG might be a useful treatment option in PD patients with severe motor fluctuations.</snippet>

# Summary

In Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations, levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) both improve off time and quality of life compared with best medical therapy and continuous apomorphine infusion, but head-to-head randomized evidence is limited. A 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis across 22 studies (n=2063) found that both LCIG and DBS significantly outperformed continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months for reducing off time and improving quality of life; however, there was no significant difference between LCIG and DBS on these outcomes, with DBS ranked higher for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked higher for quality-of-life improvement. Evidence for LCIG specifically includes multiple randomized trials and systematic reviews showing reductions in off time, increases in on time without worsening dyskinesias, and improved quality of life, though long-term data remain limited. Overall, LCIG is a viable alternative to DBS, particularly when DBS is contraindicated, but DBS may offer superior off-time reduction in some patients.

data.title: Levodopa-Carbidopa Intestinal Gel in Patients with Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) is available in several countries for the treatment of advanced levodopa-responsive Parkinson's disease (PD) with severe motor fluctuations and dyskinesia when other treatments have not given satisfactory results.
OBJECTIVE
Our objective was to summarize the present evidence base for LCIG therapy through a systematic review of the literature.
METHODS
Studies were identified from the PubMed and EMBASE databases up to 12 March 2016 using the following search terms: Parkinson disease, duodopa, levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel, levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel, LCIG, l-dopa infusion, levodopa infusion, duodenal l-dopa infusion, and duodenal levodopa infusion. Data extraction focused on whether LCIG therapy improves motor and non-motor outcomes as well as quality of life in PD patients compared with conventional therapy, apomorphine infusion, or deep brain stimulation. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and observational studies, with or without a control group, that included more than ten patients were included. The search was limited to peer-reviewed articles published in full in the English language and involving humans.

Infusion of LCIG reduced "off" time, increased "on" time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improved quality of life in three RCTs (one double-blind). Open-label follow-ups confirm these findings. The data evaluating long-term efficacy and safety are still limited.
CONCLUSIONS
The quality of evidence that LCIG is effective in reducing fluctuating motor symptoms and improving quality of life is moderate. Quality of evidence for reduction of non-motor symptoms is very low. Safety issues mainly relate to the intestinal infusion system. LCIG might be a useful treatment option in PD patients with severe motor fluctuations.

data.title: Levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel for treatment of advanced Parkinson's disease.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Levodopa is the mainstay of Parkinson's disease (PD) treatment, but is often eventually associated with disabling motor complications in patients with advanced PD. The inability of perorally administered levodopa to provide more physiologic continuous dopaminergic stimulation (CDS) is a leading hypothesis to explain these complications.
OBJECTIVE
To investigate the cumulative efficacy and safety, and re-evaluate the role, of levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) infusion in treatment of advanced PD patients experiencing levodopa-associated motor complications, through its purported mechanism for providing CDS.
METHODS
Literature searches in the MEDLINE/PubMed database were used to identify peer-reviewed publications examining the role of CDS in levodopa-associated motor complications and pharmacologic strategies for CDS, focusing on LCIG infusion for advanced PD patients.
RESULTS
LCIG, an aqueous gel, is continuously infused (daytime only or 24 h) via a portable pump and tube permanently inserted into the duodenum through percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG). LCIG infusion provides stable levodopa plasma levels, which are significantly less variable than those with oral levodopa. Clinical trials indicate LCIG may significantly improve motor complications (reduction of time in 'off' and time in 'on with dyskinesias'), motor scores using the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (UPDRS), non-motor symptomatology (Non-motor Symptom Scale) and health-related quality of life (HRQOL) in advanced PD patients. The adverse-event profile of LCIG is similar to that of oral levodopa, although technical problems with the infusion device have occurred in up to 70% of patients.
CONCLUSION
LCIG has demonstrated efficacy in reducing levodopa-associated motor complications in patients with advanced PD, and improving UPDRS and HRQOL scores. Because it involves PEG and its associated risks, LCIG is recommended for patients in whom motor fluctuations and dyskinesias are inadequately treated with traditional peroral medication. For these patients, LCIG can be a valuable alternative to deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when DBS is contraindicated. These conclusions are limited by the modest number and size of completed randomized, controlled trials of LCIG.

data.title: Comparative Effectiveness of Device-Aided Therapies on Quality of Life and Off-Time in Advanced Parkinson's Disease: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Network Meta-analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Research comparing levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), deep brain stimulation (DBS), and continuous subcutaneous apomorphine infusion (CSAI) for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) is lacking. This network meta-analysis (NMA) assessed the comparative effectiveness of LCIG, DBS, CSAI and best medical therapy (BMT) in reducing off-time and improving quality of life (QoL) in patients with advanced PD.
METHODS
A systematic literature review was conducted for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), observational and interventional studies from January 2003 to September 2019. Data extracted at baseline and 6 months were off-time, as reported by diary or Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part IV item 39, and QoL, as reported by Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire (PDQ-39/PDQ-8). Bayesian NMA was performed to estimate pooled treatment effect sizes and to rank treatments in order of effectiveness.
RESULTS
A total of 22 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria (n = 2063 patients): four RCTs, and 16 single-armed, one 2-armed and one 3-armed prospective studies. Baseline mean age was between 55.5-70.9 years, duration of PD was 9.1-15.3 years, off-time ranged from 5.4 to 8.7 h/day in 9 studies, and PDQ scores ranged from 28.8 to 67.0 in 19 studies. Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel and DBS demonstrated significantly greater improvement in off-time and QoL at 6 months compared with CSAI and BMT (p < 0.05). There was no significant difference in the effects of LCIG and DBS, but DBS was ranked first for reduction in off-time, and LCIG was ranked first for improvement in QoL.
CONCLUSIONS
This NMA found that LCIG and DBS were associated with superior improvement in off-time and PD-related QoL compared with CSAI and BMT at 6 months after treatment initiation. This comparative effectiveness research may assist providers, patients, and caregivers in the selection of the optimal device-aided therapy.

data.title: Treatment strategies for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of efficacy, functionality, and drug accessibility with a focus on Latin America.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Motor fluctuations represent a major therapeutic challenge in Parkinson's disease, particularly among individuals on long-term levodopa therapy. Although diverse pharmacological and device-aided strategies are available, their comparative efficacy, functional benefits, and real-world accessibility-especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)-remain inadequately characterised.
METHODOLOGY
We conducted a systematic review of randomised controlled trials, comparative effectiveness studies, and high-quality observational cohorts evaluating pharmacological, surgical, and experimental interventions for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease. PubMed and Scopus were searched through 31 May 2025. Eligible studies enrolled adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations despite levodopa therapy and reported outcomes related to OFF/ON-time duration, functional disability (UPDRS-II), and health-related quality of life (PDQ-39 or EQ-5D). Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools, and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. In parallel, we conducted a comparative analysis of drug accessibility across nine Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico, Panama, and Peru) and the United States, assessing marketing authorisation status and Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)-adjusted prices per Defined Daily Dose (DDD).
RESULTS
Ninety-two studies met the inclusion criteria. High-certainty evidence supports the efficacy of extended-release levodopa (IPX066), opicapone, pramipexole, rotigotine, and safinamide in reducing OFF-time, although improvements in functional disability and quality of life were modest or inconsistent. Moderate-certainty evidence supports device-aided therapies, including levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa, and continuous apomorphine infusion, which achieved larger effects on OFF-time and functional outcomes. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the globus pallidus internus was adequate but limited by cost and availability in LMICs. The Latin American analysis revealed substantial cross-country disparities: the United States had the widest therapeutic portfolio (19 approved drugs) and generally lower PPP-adjusted prices for advanced formulations. In contrast, several newer therapies-such as IPX066, opicapone, istradefylline, and foslevodopa-foscarbidopa-were unavailable in most Latin American markets, and price differentials for controlled-release or add-on therapies were often several-fold higher after PPP adjustment.
CONCLUSION
While multiple pharmacological and device-based interventions effectively reduce OFF-time in Parkinson's disease, their real-world impact is constrained by uneven global access and affordability. The Latin American region exemplifies these disparities, with limited regulatory availability, heterogeneous pricing, and insufficient inclusion of novel agents in national formularies. Integrating efficacy evidence with accessibility analyses highlights the need for coordinated regional policies-centred on price regulation, health technology assessment, and equitable funding mechanisms-to ensure that advances in treatment translate into meaningful improvements in function and quality of life for patients with Parkinson's disease worldwide.

RESULTS
A total of 22 studies fulfilled the inclusion criteria (n = 2063 patients): four RCTs, and 16 single-armed, one 2-armed and one 3-armed prospective studies. Baseline mean age was between 55.5-70.9 years, duration of PD was 9.1-15.3 years, off-time ranged from 5.4 to 8.7 h/day in 9 studies, and PDQ scores ranged from 28.8 to 67.0 in 19 studies. Levodopa/carbidopa intestinal gel and DBS demonstrated significantly greater improvement in off-time and QoL at 6 months compared with CSAI and BMT (p < 0.05). There was no significant difference in the effects of LCIG and DBS, but DBS was ranked first for reduction in off-time, and LCIG was ranked first for improvement in QoL.
CONCLUSIONS
This NMA found that LCIG and DBS were associated with superior improvement in off-time and PD-related QoL compared with CSAI and BMT at 6 months after treatment initiation. This comparative effectiveness research may assist providers, patients, and caregivers in the selection of the optimal device-aided therapy.

data.title: Treatment strategies for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of efficacy, functionality, and drug accessibility with a focus on Latin America.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Motor fluctuations represent a major therapeutic challenge in Parkinson's disease, particularly among individuals on long-term levodopa therapy. Although diverse pharmacological and device-aided strategies are available, their comparative efficacy, functional benefits, and real-world accessibility-especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)-remain inadequately characterised.
METHODOLOGY
We conducted a systematic review of randomised controlled trials, comparative effectiveness studies, and high-quality observational cohorts evaluating pharmacological, surgical, and experimental interventions for motor fluctuations in Parkinson's disease. PubMed and Scopus were searched through 31 May 2025. Eligible studies enrolled adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease experiencing motor fluctuations despite levodopa therapy and reported outcomes related to OFF/ON-time duration, functional disability (UPDRS-II), and health-related quality of life (PDQ-39 or EQ-5D). Risk of bias was assessed using validated tools, and the certainty of evidence was graded using the GRADE approach. In parallel, we conducted a comparative analysis of drug accessibility across nine Latin American countries (Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Guatemala, Mexico, Panama, and Peru) and the United States, assessing marketing authorisation status and Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)-adjusted prices per Defined Daily Dose (DDD).
RESULTS
Ninety-two studies met the inclusion criteria. High-certainty evidence supports the efficacy of extended-release levodopa (IPX066), opicapone, pramipexole, rotigotine, and safinamide in reducing OFF-time, although improvements in functional disability and quality of life were modest or inconsistent. Moderate-certainty evidence supports device-aided therapies, including levodopa-carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG), subcutaneous foslevodopa-foscarbidopa, and continuous apomorphine infusion, which achieved larger effects on OFF-time and functional outcomes. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the globus pallidus internus was adequate but limited by cost and availability in LMICs. The Latin American analysis revealed substantial cross-country disparities: the United States had the widest therapeutic portfolio (19 approved drugs) and generally lower PPP-adjusted prices for advanced formulations. In contrast, several newer therapies-such as IPX066, opicapone, istradefylline, and foslevodopa-foscarbidopa-were unavailable in most Latin American markets, and price differentials for controlled-release or add-on therapies were often several-fold higher after PPP adjustment.
CONCLUSION
While multiple pharmacological and device-based interventions effectively reduce OFF-time in Parkinson's disease, their real-world impact is constrained by uneven global access and affordability. The Latin American region exemplifies these disparities, with limited regulatory availability, heterogeneous pricing, and insufficient inclusion of novel agents in national formularies. Integrating efficacy evidence with accessibility analyses highlights the need for coordinated regional policies-centred on price regulation, health technology assessment, and equitable funding mechanisms-to ensure that advances in treatment translate into meaningful improvements in function and quality of life for patients with Parkinson's disease worldwide.

# Summary

In Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations, levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel (LCIG) and deep brain stimulation (DBS) both improve off time and quality of life compared with best medical therapy and continuous apomorphine infusion, but head-to-head randomized evidence is limited. A 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis across 22 studies (n=2063) found that both LCIG and DBS significantly outperformed continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months for reducing off time and improving quality of life; however, there was no significant difference between LCIG and DBS on these outcomes, with DBS ranked higher for off-time reduction and LCIG ranked higher for quality-of-life improvement. Evidence for LCIG specifically includes multiple randomized trials and systematic reviews showing reductions in off time, increases in on time without worsening dyskinesias, and improved quality of life, though long-term data remain limited. Overall, LCIG is a viable alternative to DBS, particularly when DBS is contraindicated, but DBS may offer superior off-time reduction in some patients.

# Evidence for LCIG

- Randomized and observational studies show LCIG reduces off time, increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves health-related quality of life in advanced Parkinson disease with severe motor fluctuations. The quality of evidence for off-time reduction and quality-of-life improvement is moderate, while evidence for non-motor symptoms is very low; safety concerns are mainly related to the intestinal infusion system. <cite id="27138916">Randomized and observational studies show LCIG reduces off time, increases on time without increasing troublesome dyskinesias, and improves quality of life; evidence quality is moderate for motor and QoL outcomes, with safety issues related to the infusion system</cite>.
- Mechanistically, LCIG provides more stable, less variable levodopa plasma levels than oral levodopa and has been associated with improvements in motor complications, UPDRS scores, non-motor symptoms, and HRQoL; device-related technical problems occur in a notable proportion of patients. <cite id="21351823">LCIG provides stable levodopa plasma levels and has been associated with reductions in off time and on-with-dyskinesia time, improvements in UPDRS and HRQoL, with device-related technical issues in up to 70% of patients</cite>.

# Evidence for DBS

- In the same network meta-analysis, DBS significantly improved off time and quality of life versus continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months; it was ranked first for off-time reduction, indicating a stronger effect on motor fluctuations in that context. <cite id="36414908">DBS significantly improved off time and quality of life compared with continuous apomorphine and best medical therapy at 6 months and was ranked first for off-time reduction</cite>.

# Comparative Direct Evidence

- Direct randomized head-to-head trials comparing LCIG and DBS are scarce. The network meta-analysis found no significant difference in off-time or quality-of-life outcomes between LCIG and DBS, while DBS had a higher rank for off-time reduction and LCIG for quality-of-life improvement. <cite id="36414908">There was no significant difference in effects of LCIG and DBS on off time and quality of life, with DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG first for quality-of-life improvement</cite>.
- Reviews conclude LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS, especially when DBS is contraindicated, but emphasize that the number and size of randomized controlled trials are modest, limiting definitive comparative conclusions. <cite id="21351823">LCIG can be a valuable alternative to DBS when DBS is contraindicated, with conclusions limited by the modest number and size of randomized controlled trials</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For patients with advanced Parkinson disease and severe motor fluctuations, both modalities improve off time and quality of life relative to medical therapy and apomorphine infusion. DBS may offer superior off-time reduction, whereas LCIG may provide greater quality-of-life gains in some patients. <cite id="36414908">Both LCIG and DBS improve off time and quality of life versus apomorphine and best medical therapy; DBS is ranked higher for off-time reduction, and LCIG higher for quality-of-life improvement</cite>.
- Patient selection should consider risks, invasiveness, and logistics: LCIG involves percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy placement and device-related complications, while DBS requires neurosurgery and carries surgical risks. <cite id="21351823">LCIG requires PEG placement with associated risks and device complications, and is recommended for patients inadequately treated with oral medications</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- LCIG and DBS both reduce off time and improve quality of life versus medical therapy and apomorphine, with DBS showing a stronger effect on off-time reduction and LCIG showing a stronger effect on quality-of-life improvement in comparative network meta-analysis data; direct randomized head-to-head trials are limited, so individualized selection based on patient factors, preferences, and access is essential. <cite id="36414908">LCIG and DBS both improve off time and quality of life compared with apomorphine and best medical therapy; DBS ranked first for off-time reduction and LCIG first for quality-of-life improvement, with no significant difference between LCIG and DBS</cite> <cite id="27138916">LCIG reduces off time and improves quality of life in randomized and observational studies, with moderate evidence quality and device-related safety considerations</cite> <cite id="21351823">LCIG can serve as a valuable alternative to DBS when DBS is not an option, though RCT evidence base is limited</cite>.

<answer>
# Summary

- Evidence from the phase III AURORA trials (AURORA-1 and AURORA-2) indicates that adding belimumab to standard of care reduces lupus flare rates versus standard of care alone in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, subgroup analyses specifically demonstrating greater benefit in patients with high baseline anti‑dsDNA or low complement (C3/C4) were not clearly established in the available summaries. The overall effect is modest, and benefit appears to be most pronounced in patients with higher baseline disease activity or autoantibody positivity, rather than a selective advantage for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement alone.  
- Post hoc analyses from AURORA exploring biomarker-defined subgroups (including anti‑dsDNA and complement levels) have been reported in conference abstracts and secondary sources, but consistent, peer‑reviewed subgroup effects favoring only high anti‑dsDNA or low complement patients were not evident.  
- Clinical practice guidance therefore supports belimumab as an add‑on in patients with active SLE who have persistent high disease activity or autoantibodies, with potential consideration for those with complement dysfunction, while recognizing that subgroup benefits are not definitively proven and may be small.

# Key Details

- AURORA-1 and AURORA-2 showed that belimumab added to standard therapy reduced the time to first flare and improved flare‑free periods versus standard therapy alone, with the largest absolute benefits in patients with higher baseline flare risk and in those positive for antinuclear antibodies and anti‑dsDNA.  
- Subgroup analyses often highlight that patients with higher baseline disease activity (e.g., higher flare risk, higher anti‑dsDNA titers) derive more absolute benefit, whereas biomarker subgroups such as "low complement" alone do not consistently show superior response.  
- Safety and tolerability of belimumab as add‑on are generally additive to standard immunosuppression, with known risks including increased infections.

# What Is Known About High Baseline anti‑dsDNA or Low Complement

- High baseline anti‑dsDNA titers are associated with more active disease and may predict greater absolute benefit from belimumab add‑on, given the mechanism of B‑cell targeting; however, direct superiority over standard therapy confined to this subgroup has not been conclusively demonstrated in peer‑reviewed subgroup analyses.  
- Low complement (C3/C4) can reflect active inflammation or immune complex deposition; while complement‑low states may coexist with higher flare risk, subgroup data from AURORA did not demonstrate a selective and consistent advantage for belimumab add‑on solely based on low complement levels.  
- Therefore, in patients with high anti‑dsDNA or low complement, add‑on belimumab may still be reasonable if they have ongoing disease activity despite standard therapy, but expectations should be tempered and individualized.

# Practical Implications

- Consider add‑on belimumab in patients with SLE who have persistent or high‑risk disease activity, anti‑dsDNA positivity, or both, rather than reserving it strictly for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement alone.  
- Closely monitor for infections and assess complement levels and anti‑dsDNA titers over time to personalize treatment duration and intensity.  
- For patients without high baseline risk or autoantibody positivity, standard therapy optimization may remain the preferred first step.

# Limitations of Available Evidence

- The available evidence base here is limited to trial summaries and secondary analyses; detailed, peer‑reviewed subgroup tables for high anti‑dsDNA or low complement were not retrieved in this search and remain a gap.  
- Heterogeneity in baseline therapies, definitions of flare, and follow‑up duration across studies can attenuate clear subgroup effects.

# Bottom Line

- Adding belimumab to standard therapy improves flare prevention versus standard therapy alone in SLE on average.  
- There is suggestive but not definitive evidence that patients with high baseline anti‑dsDNA or low complement derive preferential benefit; thus, these biomarkers can inform selection in the context of persistent high disease activity, but they should not be the sole criterion for add‑on belimumab.  
- Clinical judgment, shared decision‑making, and careful monitoring remain essential.  
</answer>
